## Why is there an operating system? {background-color="#f7f7f7"}

```text
./hello           (prints one line)     ~1,015,131 instructions
./hello_nostd     (write + exit)          ~108,573 instructions
```

The program wrote a dozen instructions.
The machine ran a hundred thousand to a million.

The rest is the operating system.

::: {.notes}
Run both with `sudo perf stat -e instructions` live. perf needs sudo.
:::

## {background-color="#f7f7f7"}

::: {style="font-size: 1.3em; text-align: center; margin-top: 1.5em;"}
The operating system is a **provider of services** ---
so it has an interface.

It is an **enforcer of isolation** ---
so that interface is a boundary, not a function call.
:::

## Today

1. What is the OS **made of**?
1. How do you **talk to** it? (the system call interface)
1. What makes the boundary a **boundary**? (hardware modes)
1. The boundary is **expensive** --- how do you pay less?
1. Where should the **code live**? (OS types, virtualization)

## An OS you cannot link, cannot trust

A library --- but not linked into your program, and shared by every program at once.

A normal library trusts its caller. The kernel must not: its callers are every program on the machine, and some are hostile.

**Unikernel: the smallest an OS can be**

```text
c-hello_qemu-x86_64      241K       855 symbols
```

240 KB to print one line. "Run a program on a machine" is a big job.

## OS types

![](../media/01-make-os/os-types.svg){fig-align="center" width="72%"}

Monolithic (all in the kernel) · microkernel (drivers are processes) · unikernel (no boundary)

## The system call is the interface

```text
$ strace ./read_write_syscall
write(1, "Gimme message: ", 15)   = 15
read(0, "hello there\n", 64)      = 12
write(1, "hello there\n", 12)     = 12
exit_group(0)                     = ?
```

Call number in `rax`, args in registers, `syscall`, result in `rax`.

The trace **is** the program. Nothing sits between it and the kernel.

::: {.notes}
Run it, type a line, then strace it. Best demo of the first half.
:::

## libc calls are not system calls

Programs call `printf()`, `malloc()`. libc turns those into system calls --- when it has to.

* `getpid()` --- one system call
* `strlen()` --- none, ever
* `printf()` --- a `write()`, or nothing, depending on the buffer

libc **decides** when to cross. That is what optimisation exploits.

## The boundary is in silicon

```text
$ ./cli
first
Segmentation fault (core dumped)
```

`cli` disables interrupts --- ring 0 only.

There is no check for it in the kernel. The **CPU** faults on it at ring 3.

A software check can have a bug. This cannot.

::: {.notes}
Then run `sudo ./cli` and show it crashes identically -- next slide, live.
:::

## Mode is not identity

![](../media/03-privileged-domain/domains-vs-privilege.svg){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

kernel/user = a hardware mode · root/non-root = a software identity

Root still runs in user mode. Root still faults on `cli`.

## What the boundary costs

```text
./make_syscalls    (write to /dev/null)   703224 us
./make_libcalls    (a function call)        9360 us
```

~70x. `/dev/null` does nothing --- almost all of it is the crossing.

**So: cross it less.**

## Two ways to cross less

```text
fwrite_buffered      65846 us          sendfile server    ~1800 us
fwrite_unbuffered  1508197 us          write server       ~5900 us
```

**Down** --- buffer in user space, batch the crossings.

**Up** --- push the whole job into the kernel, remove them.

One idea, two ends.

## Where should the code live?

* **Microkernel** --- drivers are processes. Safe, but every filesystem call is now a crossing.
* **Monolithic** --- everything privileged, one address space. Fast, but a driver bug is a kernel bug.
* **Unikernel** --- no boundary; isolation from outside.

No correct answer. Linux is monolithic; seL4 flies aircraft.

## Virtualization

![](../media/06-virtualization/virtualization.svg){fig-align="center" width="58%"}

A **hypervisor** is to operating systems what an OS is to applications.

More privileged than the kernel. Each guest OS believes it owns the machine.

## {background-color="#f7f7f7"}

::: {style="font-size: 1.25em; text-align: center; margin-top: 1.5em;"}
Dual role: provider of services, enforcer of isolation.

Isolation needs a boundary.
The boundary is entered through system calls, it costs,
and OS types and virtualization are where you put it.
:::
